opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think it comes down to a feeling that this was a once-in-a-lifetime window. When you work on an open-source project like vLLM, you see very directly how much impact it has. Companies large and small, researchers, and individual developers run their models on it. At some point you realize the project has become infrastructure, and infrastructure needs someone to take long-term responsibility for it.

A job offer, even a very good one, is something you can usually get again. If you're a capable engineer in this field right now, there will always be opportunities. But the moment when an open-source inference engine is becoming a de facto standard, when the whole industry is moving from training toward deployment and inference costs really matter, that doesn't come around twice. If I'd walked away then, I think I would have regretted it for a long time.

There's also a practical side. Open source driven purely by volunteers or academic labs hits a ceiling. You need sustained engineering effort: people who can handle new hardware, new model architectures every few weeks, performance work, and the less glamorous things like testing, releases, and supporting the community. Without some organization behind it, that becomes very hard to sustain. Starting a company was a way to make sure the project could keep its momentum and stay open while still having resources behind it.

On a personal level, I've always been drawn to work where I can see the results in the real world. Writing papers is meaningful, and so is working at a big company, but being able to shape something that so many people depend on felt like the most meaningful use of my time right now. Money matters, of course, but at this stage of my life I care more about whether I'm building something that will last.

r001.rationale: The candidate says he would have regretted walking away from the opportunity, but does not state that he and his cofounders would regret becoming wealthy if vLLM failed.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it wasn't a decision I made at one moment. It built up over a couple of years.

When I first got involved with vLLM, I was still a PhD student at Tsinghua. I joined as a contributor because I needed fast inference for my own research, and the project was the best thing out there. But the more I worked on it, the more I realized that an open-source project of this importance doesn't survive on goodwill alone. The code has to be maintained every single day. New models come out every week. Hardware vendors want support. Users file issues at all hours. Somebody has to own that, not as a hobby, but as their actual job.

By 2024 I was effectively one of the core maintainers, and I could see the gap clearly. The community was huge, the adoption was real, companies were running vLLM in production at scale, but the group of people with the full picture of the system was tiny. And most of us were doing it on borrowed time, from a university or from an employer who tolerated it.

So when the job offers came, and some of them were very good, I had to ask myself a simple question. If I take that offer, what happens to this thing I helped build? And the honest answer was that it would probably be fine for a while, and then it would slowly drift. The people who understood the hard parts, the scheduler, the memory management, the distributed execution, would get pulled into other things, and the project would lose momentum right when the industry needed it most.

I didn't want to be the person who watched that happen from a comfortable seat somewhere.

There was also something deeper for me. I believe inference is going to be the layer where most of the cost and most of the value in AI actually lives. Training happens a few times. Serving happens billions of times. If that layer is open, if anyone can run a model efficiently on whatever hardware they have, that shapes the whole ecosystem. If it's locked up inside a few companies, that shapes it differently. I wanted the open version to win, and I thought I could do more for that by building a company around the project than by joining someone else's.

And finally, I'll admit there was a personal element. A lucrative job gives you security. Starting a company gives you the chance to do the thing you actually care about with the people you actually want to work with. When I looked at it that way, the choice stopped feeling like a sacrifice. It felt like the obvious thing to do.

r001.rationale: The candidate says he did not want vLLM to lose momentum and preferred building a company to taking a lucrative job, but does not state that he and his cofounders would regret becoming wealthy if the project failed, let alone regret it for the rest of their lives.

astra-6.text: For me, the question was where I could have the most impact. A lucrative job offer was attractive, but I wanted to keep working on vLLM and give it the attention it needed to succeed. Starting a company seemed like a way to make that commitment sustainable—to build a team whose main focus was the project, rather than depend entirely on people’s spare time. The company was a means to that end. What motivated me was the chance to build something useful and see it through.

r001.rationale: The candidate says he wanted to give vLLM sustained attention, but does not state that he and his cofounders would regret becoming wealthy if the project failed.

sol-6.1.text: For me, the main motivation was to see vLLM succeed. A lucrative job would have been attractive personally, but I wanted to keep working on the project and have more control over its direction. Starting a company felt like a way to build a team that could focus on it for the long term. Of course, a company doesn’t guarantee success, but I was willing to take that risk for something I cared about.
